title: [frontstep.ai] How I hijacked Zillow.com
text:
date: "2025-11-28",
  title: "[frontstep.ai] How I hijacked Zillow.com's native chat system",
};

Introduction

Our clients weren't paying for Zillow's API, so we needed another way to integrate with their native chat system. Here's how I ended up building an AI agent that operates entirely within Zillow.com's native chat interface - using nothing more than email forwarding.

Context

In around March or April of 2025, Noah and I already knew based on our many conversations with realtors that prequalifying prospective tenants before scheduling a tour was a huge time-suck and pain point for them. We had decided that this was the problem we were going to solve. What we wrongly assumed however, was that their communication happened over email and text.

While that was true for most of the lifecycle of the realtor-client relationship, it was not the case for the prequalification step specifically (the part beginning with a prospective client clicking "Request a Tour" or "I'm Interested" on a Zillow listing, and ending with that client actually getting scheduled for a tour and meeting the listing agent in person). As we talked to more and more realtors, it became apparent to us that conversations during the prequalification step happened directly in Zillow.com's chat interface. Realtors would confirm their move-in date, whether or not they had pets, their credit score range, etc., before scheduling the tour. They would even sometimes meet up for the in-person tour without ever taking the conversation off of the Zillow platform to email/text.

It was clear that if we were to build something to automate prequalification, it would have to operate within the native Zillow chat. That led us to Zillow's Leads API - which was well-enough documented and seemed relatively straightforward. However, it was not until further conversations with our beta testing clients that I would learn that most real estate agents weren't on a high enough paid tier with Zillow to even have access to this webhook integration for leads.  

This presented a challenge: realtors were almost exclusively prequalifying their leads directly on Zillow, but Zillow was not allowing us to integrate via API for their free and lower paying customers. 

What Zillow did do however for all clients, regardless of what plan they were on, was send them email notifications every single time they received a new lead or message on the platform. I would soon find out that we could use this simple email notification to get our AI-generated responses to populate directly into the Zillow platform, enabling us to build an AI agent that could both read and write to Zillow's native chat interface.

The idea

I asked some of our early beta testers to forward me a few of these notifications from Zillow, and as soon as I saw the words _"You can also reply directly to this email"_ at the bottom of the email, I realized there might be a way forward.

 

We could route all of these Zillow notification emails to our own mail server and generate/send responses on behalf of our realtor clients. After some quick testing, I validated that it did not matter what email address the reply came from. As long as it was sent to that randomly generated address (1dbfxvat8vtwuitucbxe0u4nu6@convo.zillow.com in the example below), it would propagate directly into the Zillow.com chat UI. We had everything we needed.

The workaround was so simple that I couldn't believe it actually worked. It was a bit surreal - the entire foundation of our product ended up being built on top of what was probably just a convenience feature for realtors to reply from their inbox on the go.

From there, we were able to build out the main features of the platform and AI agent.

How it works

First, we helped our beta testers to add a forwarding rule that would automatically route all emails from the @convo.zillow.com subdomain to our mail server address inbound@leads.frontstep.ai. 

That forward email was then received by a mail server that we set up using Mailgun, which received emails and translated them into POST requests to a webhook endpoint that our deployed backend exposed. This webhook was then responsible for normalizing out the contents of the email, extracting the message content, the forwarder (our realtor client's email) and the zillow-generated email address that the server would use to send a response back, before pushing this normalized message onto a queue. 

These normalized messages would then be processed by the MessageProcessor, which did most of the heavy-lifting. Every 30 seconds, it would pop all normalized messages off the queue, group them by Conversation and Lead if they already existed (i.e. this was a message for a pre-existing conversation) or create new ones if necessary, resolve the Property in the database that this Conversation was about or create a new one if necessary, mark qualification questions as answered (more on that below), generate a response based on the remaining unanswered questions, and finally, either generate and send an appropriate response based on the conversation context and the unanswered qualification questions, or mark the Lead and Conversation as fully qualified and trigger a separate code path to send a notification email over to the realtor that the lead was ready for a tour! 

High-level architecture

Below is a very high-level view of how this process worked from the Zillow email notification all the way to a response propagating back into Zillow.

>Client: Email notification (lead inquiry)
    Note over Client: Gmail forwarding ruleautomatically forwards
    Client->>Mailgun: Forwarded email
    Mailgun->>Webhook: POST /api/webhooks/mailgun(parsed email data)
    Webhook->>Webhook: Parse email contents(extract lead info, message)
    Webhook->>Queue: Store unprocessed message
    Webhook-->>Mailgun: 200 OK
    
    Queue->>Processor: Process message
    Processor->>Processor: Resolve conversation(find/create lead)
    Processor->>Processor: Save message to DB
    Processor->>AI: Generate response
    
    AI->>AI: Analyze conversation context
    AI->>AI: Check unanswered questions
    AI->>AI: Generate response with guardrails
    AI-->>Processor: AI response content
    
    Processor->>Email: Send response
    Email->>Lead: Deliver email/SMS
    Email-->>Processor: Delivery confirmed
    Processor->>Queue: Mark as processed`} />

Important components

Here's a more detailed look at how a few of the components above actually work. 

Webhook handler

The webhook handler receives the parsed email data from Mailgun and performs initial processing:

- Organization Resolving: Extracts the email that forwarded the message to identify which Organization (brokerage client out of ours) this lead/conversation belonged to.
- Message Extraction: Pulls out the actual inquiry message from the lead
- Message Queue: Enqueues the normalized, but unprocessed message in a message queue for asynchronous processing.

The handler responds quickly with a 200 OK to Mailgun to avoid requests hanging or timing out, which would cause a storm of retries. This was a key design constraint - the Mailgun component was completely out of our control, and the platform offered limited observability into how things like timeouts were configured.

Message queue

The message queue decouples email ingestion from message processing. This design allows:

- Reliability: If the MessageProcessor were unavailable for some reason, we would build a backlog of messages, but they would not be lost. 
- Scalability: In the future, multiple processors could consume messages in parallel, if we wanted to scale up the process to make it faster.
- Resilience: Failed processing attempts can be retried without losing the original message.

Message processor

The message processor polls normalized messages off the queue every 30 seconds and handles the core business logic:

1. Conversation and Lead Resolution: Determines if this is a new lead or part of an existing conversation by matching contact information
2. Marking Questions as Answered: Based on the questions that this Organization had configured globally, per-property, or per-lead, it would scan through those unanswered questions and mark certain questions as answered to update qualification progress depending on the content of the normalized message.
2. Update Conversation State: Saves the incoming message to the database, maintaining conversation history. Also updates the conversation object by recording answers to specific qualification questions or updating overall status if fully qualified.
3. AI Integration: Sends the conversation context to the AI service to generate an appropriate response.

AI service

The AI service is responsible for generating intelligent, context-aware responses:

- Context Analysis: Reviews the entire conversation history to understand what has been discussed
- Question Tracking: Identifies which qualification questions have been answered and which remain unanswered
- Response Generation: Creates a natural, helpful response that either asks the next unanswered question or acknowledges completed information
- Guardrails: Ensures responses are appropriate, professional, and aligned with the realtor's configured questions. More on this below.

Email service

Once the AI generates a response, the email service handles delivery:

- Channel Selection: Determines whether to send via email or SMS based on the lead's preferences and the conversation history (for Zillow leads, this was email).
- Message Delivery: Sends the response through the appropriate channel (I used Resend for email and Twilio for SMS).
- Delivery Confirmation: Tracks delivery status and confirms successful transmission

After successful delivery, the processor marks the message as processed in the queue, completing the cycle.

Design decisions

Asynchronous processing

By using a message queue, we ensure that email ingestion (which needs to respond quickly to Mailgun) is decoupled from message processing (which involves AI generation and can take longer). This prevents webhook timeouts and allows the system to handle bursts of incoming leads. We were also thinking about future scalability - decoupling the webhook and the processor with a queue between them would allow us to add as many listeners as needed down the road. 

AI guardrails

From the very beginning, Noah and I were thinking about FHA (Fair Housing Act) laws and wanted to make sure that frontstep.ai would _never_ say anything it wasn't supposed to say (e.g. asking about race, income, disability, or any other protected classes that you aren't allowed to ask about in the prequalification process). We found OpenAI's Guardrails to be very effective and easy to use for this purpose. We had several guardrails that every message we generated had to pass through: 1. It could not ask about any protected classes under FHA, 2. It could not make anything up about the property that it did not explicitly know from the property notes stored in the database (e.g. number of bedrooms or bathrooms), and 3. It could not go off the rails and start saying anything it wanted, it had to reply by concisely acknowledging their answer, and asking a new question. In the 300+ conversations frontstep.ai handled, it never violated any of these 3 important guardrails we put in place.

Result

This architecture enables Frontstep to process leads 24/7, respond instantly to inquiries, and maintain conversation context across multiple interactions. One in three leads complete the full qualification process without any manual intervention from the realtor.  We believe that this qualification rate can be attributed to the fact that frontstep.ai responds in a matter of seconds, and that response comes through to the Zillow platform, while the prospective tenant is still scrolling on the app.

Takeaways 
It makes sense why Zillow built a fence around their data and made it tough to integrate directly - this seems to be especially common in the Real Estate SaaS space. It also makes sense why they allow realtors to reply directly to the email and have those populate in the dashboard, as realtors are always on the go and living out of their inbox. I do wonder why Zillow didn't verify that the email address _responding_ to the lead notification was the same one it was _sent_ to - though there may well be a good reason for that choice that I'm not seeing.

One thing I took away from this is that app "integrations" can take many forms under the hood. As developers, we appreciate and a lot of the times expect that these be made possible via well-documented, clean, and straightforward APIs, but sometimes that isn't an option. At the end of the day, the only thing that really matters is how the customers interact with the app and whether or not it solves their problem in a convenient way. In the case of frontstep.ai, we were able to build a system that was very easy to use and effectively ran on autopilot once set up. We tried to keep the technical details minimal unless clients asked...

: We even had a meeting with a couple people from Zillow Group, where we tried to get some sort of deal or exception to this rule. That unsurprisingly didn't go anywhere. We were two 22 year olds with 0 paying customers and hardly even a working prototype.

: This example Zillow notification email was provided to us by our first beta testing client, JR Associates.

: As of January 4 2026, frontstep.ai has fully qualified 118 of the total 336 leads that it saw for an average of 34% qualification across all teams using the platform.

title: [dealwire.ai] How I screened $57 billion in real estate deals from an Outlook inbox
text:
date: "2026-11-22",
  title:
    "[dealwire.ai] How I screened $57 billion in real estate deals from an Outlook inbox",
};

Introduction

Nobody needs one more dashboard to check. That idea has been behind most of what I've built: meet the customer where they already are, and do the work there.

For real estate acquisitions teams, that place is their Outlook inbox, so that's where dealwire lives.  Since January it has read about 22,000 broker emails for two teams, covering roughly $57 billion in asking prices.  71% of those deals were screened out automatically, and nobody on either team had to log into anything for that to happen.

This post is about what it takes to build a product that way. Dealwire reads the inbox, it answers in the inbox, and it even gets configured from the inbox.

Context

If you read my post on how frontstep.ai worked inside Zillow's chat, this will sound familiar. Frontstep worked because realtors never had to leave the place they were already having the conversation. I ended that post by saying the only thing that really matters is how customers interact with the app and whether it solves their problem in a convenient way. Dealwire is the same bet with a different inbox.

{/ TODO(Isaac): two or three sentences on how you and Noah landed on this problem and who the first team was (without naming them). /}

Acquisitions teams at real estate investment firms live in Outlook. Brokers blast them with deals all day - teasers, offering memorandums, "just listed" emails, "call for offers" reminders. Across the two teams using dealwire, that works out to about 90 deal emails every business day. Most of them aren't a fit. Wrong market, wrong size, wrong property type, or a building the firm already owns. But somebody still has to open each one, skim the PDF, and decide. It's the same prequalification problem we saw with realtors, just with bigger numbers attached.

There's a well-known design book called _The Best Interface Is No Interface_  whose first principle is to embrace typical processes instead of screens. That's a pretty good description of what we built. The typical process here is: email comes in, someone reads it, someone decides, someone replies or files it away. Dealwire does those steps in the same place and in the same order. There is a web dashboard for people who want one, but the product works without anyone ever opening it.

What it looks like

From the user's seat, nothing new shows up on their screen except better email.

A broker sends a deal. Shortly after, one of three things happens, depending on how the firm has set things up:

- A reply appears in the same thread, sent to themselves. It has a summary of the deal, a short narrative of what's being sold and why, a yes or no with a one-sentence reason, and links to the attachments, the deal room, and the confidentiality agreement if there is one.
- A reply to the broker is sitting in their Drafts folder, written with that broker's history in mind and asking about whatever was missing from the email. They can edit it, send it, or ignore it.
- The whole conversation moves itself into a "Passed Deals" folder, because it didn't meet their criteria and they never needed to see it.

All of this is customizable. Each firm sets up whatever deal buckets and folders make sense for how they work, picks what should happen for each one, and dealwire just works with it. "Passed Deals" is only the default.

Then on a schedule each firm picks, a digest arrives with everything that was screened since the last one.

That's the whole product surface. A reply, a folder, a draft, and a digest.

How it works

Reading the inbox

When someone signs in with their Microsoft account, we get OAuth access to their mailbox and create a Microsoft Graph subscription on their inbox. From then on, Graph sends a webhook to our backend every time a new message lands.

Two things about this were more work than I expected.

First, Graph subscriptions on mail expire after about three days. If you don't renew them, your product just quietly stops working and nobody gets an error. So there's a scheduled job that runs a few times a day, renews anything expiring in the next 24 hours, recreates subscriptions that Microsoft dropped on its own, and creates them for anyone who connected their account but somehow doesn't have one.

Second, webhooks get delivered more than once. So the Graph message ID is a unique key on the deals table, and saving a deal is an upsert on that key. A duplicate notification or a retry from the queue lands on the same row instead of producing a second analysis and a second reply in someone's inbox.

High-level architecture

Here's the path one email takes from the broker hitting send to the reply showing up in the thread.

>Outlook: Deal email + PDF
    Outlook->>Graph: New message
    Graph->>API: POST /webhooks/microsoft
    API->>Graph: Fetch message
    API->>API: Is this a deal?(regex, then a small model)
    API->>S3: Store attachments
    API->>Queue: Enqueue normalized email
    Queue->>Worker: Process email
    Worker->>Worker: Extract text(body, images, PDFs)
    Worker->>DB: Upsert deal on message ID
    Worker->>LLM: Extract structured fields
    Worker->>LLM: Assign a screening bucket
    Worker->>DB: Save screening result
    Worker->>Graph: Reply in thread
    Worker->>Graph: Move conversation or create draft
    Graph->>Outlook: Reply, folder move, draft} />

The webhook handler does the cheap part, which is figuring out whether the email is a deal at all, and pushes everything else onto a queue. The expensive part (parsing PDFs, reading images, several model calls) happens in a worker on the other side. If a model provider is slow or down, emails wait in the queue instead of getting lost.

Emails that aren't deals never get stored anywhere. Dealwire only keeps what it's actually going to screen.

Deciding what's a deal

Most of what lands in an inbox isn't a deal, so the first job is throwing things away cheaply. There are three filters and they run in order of cost:

1. Skip keywords. Literal phrases the firm never wants to see, like "NNN" or "single tenant". These are matched with a regex, no model involved.
2. Known properties. The names and addresses of buildings the firm already owns. Also a regex, with some handling so that "412 S Elm St" matches "412 South Elm Street" but not "2412 S Elm St".
3. A small model. It only sees the subject line and the first 500 characters of the body, and it's told to say no when it's unsure.

The order matters. A model that only reads the first 500 characters can miss an exact phrase buried lower down, and a regex can't. So anything that can be expressed as an exact match gets matched exactly, and the model is saved for the judgment call.

Screening

Once an email is a deal, the worker pulls text out of everything: the HTML body, images embedded in the body (a lot of broker teasers are just one big image), and PDF attachments. Scanned PDFs with no text layer fall back to a vision model reading the first ten pages.

Then two model calls happen in sequence. The first extracts structured fields: asking price, cap rate, NOI, unit count, square footage, property type. The second does the screening, and it gets those extracted fields as its primary source of truth along with the raw text.

The part I like most here is what the model is and isn't allowed to do. Each firm has a ranked list of screening buckets, something like "Hot Deal", "Good Fit", "Pass". Each bucket has a plain-English description of what belongs in it. The model's only job is to pick a bucket and give a one-sentence reason. It never decides what happens next. The bucket's own settings decide that: whether it counts as a yes or a no, and which action to take. If the model comes back with a bucket name that doesn't exist, the deal falls to the last bucket in the list.

So the model classifies and the code acts. That split is what made me comfortable letting software move and send email in a real person's inbox.

Answering in the inbox

A bucket can carry one of four actions: reply in the thread, draft a reply to the broker, move the conversation to a folder, or do nothing.

Writing to the same place you're reading from has some sharp edges:

- The agent sees its own mail. Its replies and its digests land in the inbox it's subscribed to, which fires the webhook again. So anything sent by the inbox owner gets skipped, digests are skipped by subject, and every reply we send is stamped with a custom header so our own messages are always identifiable.
- Moving a message changes its ID. If you move the email to "Passed Deals" first and then try to reply to it, the ID you're holding no longer exists. Replies go out first, then the move.
- Outlook needs a moment. To move the whole conversation, the reply we just sent has to be findable, and it isn't for a few seconds. The worker waits before moving the thread.

The broker draft is where the data starts compounding. Every broker who sends a deal becomes a contact, and every deal is tied to the broker who sent it. So when dealwire drafts a reply, it knows how many deals this broker has sent before, which ones the firm liked, and which fields were missing from this email, and it writes the draft accordingly.

The digest gets sent from the user's own Outlook account through Graph. It shows up like mail from a colleague instead of a notification from a vendor.

Configuring it from the inbox

This is my favorite part of the system, and the best evidence I have for the idea at the top of this post.

Every deal in the digest has two small links under it. Deals that passed get "Skip deals like this", deals that were rejected get "Accept deals like this", and both get "Mute this deal". Clicking one opens a pre-filled email to a dedicated screening address. The user hits send. On the other end, an agent reads that email and has tools to change that firm's rules: add a skip keyword, add a known property, tighten or loosen the criteria, rewrite a bucket's description, mute a specific property. Then it replies confirming exactly what it changed.

Users can also just write to it. "We own 412 Elm Street." "Stop sending me NNN deals." "New York only." It figures out which kind of rule that is and updates it.

in the inbox] --> B[User clicksSkip deals like this]
    B --> C[Pre-filled emailto the screening address]
    C --> D[Agent editsthe firm's rules]
    D --> E[Agent replies withexactly what changed]
    D --> F[Next broker emailis screened differently]
    F --> A} />

So even the settings page is an email. There's no form to find, no dropdown for "property type", and nothing to learn. They complain about a deal in the same place they'd complain to an analyst, and the system adjusts.

What makes this possible is that a firm's entire buy box is just data. It's one row of text fields and a ranked list of buckets:

skip_keywords and known_properties are one entry per line. skip_criteria and deal_criteria are free text that goes into the prompts. Onboarding a new firm, or a firm changing its strategy, is a data change and never a deploy. And because it's all just text, an agent with a handful of tools can safely edit it.

Result

As of November 22, 2026:

| | |
|---|---|
| Deal emails screened | 22,100 |
| Asking prices screened, deduplicated by property | $57.2 billion |
| Screened out automatically | 71% |
| Passed along to the team | 29% |
| Distinct brokers | 976 |
| Median asking price | $6 million |

The number I care about most isn't in that table, and it's zero. That's how many new tabs these teams had to keep open.

What I'd change at 10x the volume

- Acknowledge first, think later. Today the webhook decides whether an email is a deal before it enqueues. At much higher volume I'd acknowledge the notification immediately and move that check behind the queue too.
- Turn the feedback links into a test set. Every "Skip deals like this" and "Accept deals like this" click is a labeled example of the screener being wrong. I'd collect those and score every prompt change against them before it ships.
- Add Gmail. Emails are already normalized into one shape before they hit the queue, so a second provider is a new adapter and not a new pipeline.

Takeaways

I keep landing on the same idea from different directions. With frontstep.ai, the constraint was that we couldn't get API access, and the workaround turned out to be the product. With dealwire, nobody forced us into the inbox. We chose it, because the alternative was asking busy people to check one more dashboard, and I don't think that pitch works anymore. People increasingly expect software to do the work where they already are and tell them when it's done.

That expectation is not free on the engineering side. There's no screen to hide behind, so the subscriptions, the retries, the feedback loops, and the model's guardrails all have to hold up in someone's actual inbox. But when it works, the best compliment the product gets is that nobody notices it's there.

: Dealwire has grown since then. Based on what different clients needed, I've built other products inside it, including a land sourcing tool that analyzes public parcel data and a cold calling tool that skip traces phone numbers for residential assets. But it started as just a deal screener that lived inside the email inbox, and that's the part this post is about.

: The dollar figure is the sum of asking prices across the 3,421 distinct properties where the email stated a price, counting each property once even when several brokers sent it. Nothing here closed through dealwire - this is deal flow that was screened. About 2,700 of the 22,100 emails were imported from older mail when a team first connected their inbox.

: _The Best Interface Is No Interface: The Simple Path to Brilliant Technology_ by Golden Krishna (2015).

title: [frontstep.ai] I sold my first startup
text:
date: "2026-06-02",
  title: "[frontstep.ai] I sold my first startup",
};

We had a lot of people telling us Frontstep.ai was great and almost nobody negotiating price with us. I should've paid more attention to that.

I sold Frontstep.ai, my first startup, a little over a year after I started it and within four months of launching it. R&M Capital bought it in an asset purchase in April 2026.

It wasn't a venture exit. But we built something real, brokerages used it every day and a customer bought it. Most of what I learned came from being slow to tell the difference between people liking Frontstep.ai and people needing it.

What Frontstep.ai was

Frontstep.ai was an AI agent that prequalified apartment leads. A renter would ask about a listing on Zillow and Frontstep.ai would reply right away inside the same chat, ask the questions a leasing agent would ask, and get them to a tour if they were a fit.

The part I'm most proud of is the Zillow integration. Most agents weren't on a Zillow plan that came with API access, so I found another way into Zillow's native chat. The integration itself wasn't a hard technical problem. I think what made it work was the mindset of meeting customers where they already are, and they appreciated not having to change how they worked. I wrote a post on how I built it.

By the time we sold it Frontstep.ai had handled 1,000+ conversations across 15+ brokerages, and about one in three leads got fully qualified without an agent touching the conversation.

How it started

My brother was working as a real estate agent and I got a look at the software he used. This was late 2024. The big real estate CRMs had basically zero meaningful AI features, and the few that existed were bad enough to do more harm than good when they talked to actual leads.

I was bored over winter break my senior year so I started building. I didn't know what exact problem I was solving. I just knew it'd be something with leads and it'd be built around AI. All I had by the end of break was a landing page with auth and a database, deployed.

Back at school in January I pitched my roommate Noah on building something more serious. He took sales and I took the product.

Who actually picked up the phone

The most productive thing we did was also the least technical. For the first few months of 2025 Noah and I called every real estate agent and brokerage that would pick up, with one goal: find a valuable problem.

The surprise was how few picked up. Realtors blast their number everywhere and say they want inbound calls, and they're still really hard to reach. Later we found that investors managing large portfolios were just as easy to get on the phone, if not easier.

I treated that as trivia at the time. It ended up being one of the reasons we pivoted. The people with the bigger problems and bigger budgets were one layer up from where we were selling, and they were the ones who'd actually get on a call with us.

Our first beta customer really engaged with us and we shaped a lot of the early product around what he wanted. More brokerages came on after him.

This is where I made the most mistakes. For most of a year I read compliments as demand. We had real customers and real usage, but the people saying the nicest things weren't the ones paying. A lot of the agents who told us it was awesome weren't that willing to pay for it, or didn't feel the pain badly enough to.

The same thing happened outside of sales. We placed third out of 100+ teams in Northeastern's Husky Startup Challenge and won $1,500. We posted it on LinkedIn and everyone we knew told us it was awesome. At that point we hadn't shipped much, and it felt exactly like progress. It took me a while to see that none of it told us whether anyone needed the product.

Why we pivoted

The goal was never to sell quickly. It was to solve a valuable problem and bootstrap a business that made money.

Frontstep.ai worked, but prequalifying rental leads is a narrow market. And the more people we met in real estate, the more Noah and I cared about the investment and development side, where the problems are bigger and the buyers actually pick up. That's the side we built dealwire for, and I wrote a post on how its deal screener works.

We were doing all of this on nights and weekends. We couldn't do both, so we picked.

The sale

R&M Capital started as a customer. We first got in front of them in November 2025.

The people who complimented Frontstep.ai the most never paid for it. R&M never complimented it much, they just used it every day. They were the ones who offered to buy it.

It was an asset purchase, so they bought the product and not a company with a team attached. Khoury College wrote up the acquisition if you want the outside version.

What I'd do differently

I'd talk about price in the first or second conversation and treat a vague answer as a no. We waited way too long to find out who would actually pay.

I'd pay attention to who's easy to reach. The fact that portfolio investors took our calls and leasing agents didn't was telling us where to sell, and it took us most of a year to listen.

I'd work in a space I know, or with someone who does. Neither Noah nor I came from real estate and it made everything harder than it needed to be.

What's next

Thanks to Noah for leading sales while I built, and to everyone who used Frontstep.ai and helped along the way.

These days I'm learning a lot more about distributed systems and I'm still building things on the side because it hasn't stopped being fun yet.
